item.title: World shares are mixed as Nvidia's troubles weigh on AI stocks
item.description: World shares were mixed on Thursday as concerns over leadership at chipmaker Nvidia weighed on artificial intelligence-related stocks.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: TOKYO — World shares were mixed on Thursday as concerns over leadership at chipmaker Nvidia weighed on artificial intelligence-related stocks. In after-hours trading, Nvidia’s shares fell 8.6 per cent after reports said Nvidia’s board was meeting late Wednesday to discuss the situation surrounding its CEO, Jensen Huang, whose affair with a Chinese woman has raised national security concerns in the U.S. Nvidia ‘s shares climbed 2.9 per cent on Wednesday. Its shares have fallen after the company said it was investigating Huang, who has admitted to a relationship with a businesswoman who reportedly fed intelligence and advanced chips to China. The future for the S&P 500 slipped 0.4 per cent, while that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average was nearly unchanged. In early European trading, France’s CAC 40 added 0.7 per cent and the German DAX rose 1.0 per cent to 26,939.92. Britain’s FTSE 100 jumped 0.3 per cent to 10,868.98. In Asian trading, Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 shed 0.7 per cent to 60,819.36. In South Korea, the Kospi gave up early gains to slip 0.6 per cent to 5,342.73. Taiwan’s Taiex lost 2.6 per cent. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 declined nearly 0.1 per cent to 9,146.80. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng lost 1.3 per cent to 24,008.55, while the Shanghai Composite fell 0.7 per cent to 3,655.83. Apart from Nvidia’s situation, investors are worried about a potential slowdown in the overall AI industry given longstanding questions about whether it will prove profitable enough to make massive investments in the technology worthwhile. Analysts also said people might still be taking a risk, snatching up Nvidia shares at what appears to be a discount because of uncertainty over what Huang’s woes might mean for the company. “There is no credible way to put a precise revenue loss on his departure,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote. “Customers buy Nvidia’s computing power, software and networking ecosystem, and those advantages wouldn’t disappear with its CEO,” she said. Benchmark U.S. crude rose 0.8 per cent to US$87.26 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, added 0.8 per cent to $93.53 a barrel. Brent has vacillated within a range of $72 to $120 since the war with Iran pushed prices much higher. In currency trading, the U.S. dollar fell to 159.64 Japanese yen from 159.79 yen. The euro cost $1.1095, up from $1.1091. ___ Yuri Kageyama, The Associated Press

item.title: Joly set to hold meeting in Toronto with Stellantis, union and Ontario minister
item.description: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is set to hold a four-way meeting today with automaker Stellantis, the union representing its more than 9,000 workers in Canada, and representatives of the Ontario ...
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is set to hold a four-way meeting today with automaker Stellantis, the union representing its more than 9,000 workers in Canada, and representatives of the Ontario government. The discussions in Toronto come days after Stellantis announced it was selling its Brampton, Ont. assembly plant to Canadian armoured vehicle manufacturer Roshel for an undisclosed amount. More than 2,000 workers have been laid off from the plant since it was idled in 2023. Collective bargaining negotiations between Stellantis and Unifor broke down in September after the automaker signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel to target a sale of the facility. Unifor national president Lana Payne has called the sale a “worst-case scenario,” as she says Stellantis “betrayed our members with an underhanded deal to sell the plant and walk away from its commitments to these workers.” Joly’s office denied reports late Wednesday that she was involved in negotiations that led to the deal, saying the minister never met with Roshel. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026. Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

item.title: Stan Wong: Tech and AI are under pressure. Is the market missing the bigger picture?
item.description: The recent selloff in technology and artificial intelligence-related equities has raised questions about the durability of the AI infrastructure investment cycle.
item.content:encoded:
The recent selloff in technology and artificial intelligence-related equities has raised questions about the durability of the AI infrastructure investment cycle. Political uncertainty, escalating capital spending and concerns over investment returns have contributed to the correction. Yet market sentiment appears to have deteriorated more rapidly than the underlying demand for computing capacity.

At their respective lows during the recent correction, the Nasdaq-100 had fallen nearly 15 per cent from its previous peak, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had declined almost 39 per cent from its June high. Democratic victories in U.S. Congress and growing opposition to data-centre development have heightened concerns over regulation, electricity costs and permitting. Hedge fund deleveraging and the unwinding of crowded AI positions have further amplified the selling. These risks warrant scrutiny. But short-term disruptions to individual projects should not be confused with a breakdown in the structural forces driving this global investment cycle. A global investment cycle AI infrastructure is not exclusively an American growth story. Hyperscalers are expanding computing capacity across Asia, Europe and the Middle East as businesses and governments accelerate AI adoption. Microsoft, for example, announced US$10 billion of investment in Japan through 2029, covering AI infrastructure, cybersecurity, and workforce development, alongside plans for more than US$10 billion of capital and operating spending across the Middle East through 2030. The International Energy Agency projects global data-centre electricity consumption will nearly double, from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 terawatt-hours by 2030. This expansion points to substantial demand for semiconductors, power generation, cooling systems, and electrical infrastructure. U.S. political developments may influence where and when investments occur, but they do not eliminate the need for computing capacity worldwide. Investment will follow opportunity Within the United States, states and municipalities compete to attract investment, jobs, and tax revenues. Developers facing restrictions in one jurisdiction can evaluate alternatives offering reliable power, transmission capacity, suitable sites, and more predictable approvals. Relocation is neither immediate nor costless. Grid interconnections, equipment lead times and financing requirements can create delays, and some projects may be cancelled. Opposition to data centres also crosses party lines, particularly where electricity affordability, land use and water consumption are at issue. Nevertheless, constraints in individual jurisdictions are not equivalent to a nationwide halt in development. They may redistribute investment rather than eliminate demand. The strategic race with China AI leadership carries consequences for productivity, economic competitiveness, cybersecurity, and national security. Competition with China gives the United States a powerful strategic incentive to maintain investment in advanced computing, regardless of which party controls Congress. Democratic control of the incoming Congress introduces additional policy uncertainty, but presidential veto authority and legislative constraints limit the scope of immediate federal changes. State and local permitting decisions can present more direct obstacles. Distinguishing these different sources of regulatory risk is essential to assessing their impact on corporate earnings. The investment cycle is not the investment case According to Boston Consulting Group , Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle are projected to invest nearly US$3.9 trillion in AI capital expenditures between 2026 and 2030. The extraordinary scale of these commitments underscores the long-term nature of the infrastructure buildout, supporting demand across the semiconductor, electrical equipment, and power infrastructure industries. These substantial outlays also raise legitimate questions about future revenue, financing requirements, and returns on invested capital. A durable industry growth cycle does not make every AI-related stock an attractive investment. Established businesses with substantial free cash flow, strong balance sheets and visible earnings growth differ fundamentally from speculative companies reliant on external funding or unproven projects. Valuation is equally important. Strong secular demand cannot compensate for paying too much for anticipated earnings. Conversely, a sharp share-price decline does not necessarily signal deterioration in a company’s operating outlook. The opportunity lies in separating changing market sentiment from changing business fundamentals. Fundamentals matter more than headlines History provides useful perspective on severe corrections. My analysis of Bloomberg data over the past 20 years shows that following Nasdaq-100 drawdowns of 15 per cent or more, the index delivered positive 12-month returns in 75 per cent of non-overlapping episodes, with an average gain of 21.2 per cent and median gain of 31.4 per cent. The long-term investment opportunity in AI infrastructure remains compelling, but successful investing requires distinguishing structural growth from speculative excess. Periods of indiscriminate selling can create opportunities in financially sound businesses with sustainable earnings growth and reasonable valuations. Portfolio decisions must also reflect diversification, liquidity requirements, investment horizons, and risk tolerance, within the context of each client’s broader total wealth plan. item.title: CoreWeave sparks AI cloud stock rally, lifts Nvidia as results ease bubble fears
item.description: CoreWeave jumped more than 20 per cent on Wednesday, igniting a rally in battered AI cloud stocks, as its hefty spending yielded strong revenue growth and the company signaled a pullback from the ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: CoreWeave jumped more than 20 per cent on Wednesday, igniting a rally in battered AI cloud stocks, as its hefty spending yielded strong revenue growth and the company signaled a pullback from the borrowing binge that had set off alarms of an AI bubble. The earnings also helped lift shares of key CoreWeave backer Nvidia by two per cent, after a bruising two-day slide driven by worries about CEO Jensen Huang’s future at the company following his affair with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing. Shares of so-called “neoclouds” including Nebius and Iren rallied after facing weeks of turmoil on fears that their debt-fuelled data centre expansion could backfire if AI demand slows. “CoreWeave’s earnings directly addressed the fear that’s driven this whole selloff,” said Dan Sheehan, director of portfolio management at Telos Wealth Advisors. “The neocloud that became the poster child for AI financing worries took real weight off the fear that had been the heart of the selloff.” The Democratic midterm sweep last week had dealt a blow to the industry, with several winning candidates campaigning for tighter regulation and moratoriums on new data center construction, including in the crucial market of Texas. CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told Reuters on Tuesday that greater scrutiny could slow data center construction across the industry, but he did not expect it to significantly alter the company’s expansion plans or drive up costs. There will be no impact to CoreWeave’s planned capacity additions over the next year, he added. The company also said it would not tap unsecured debt markets after a recent spike in borrowing costs, and that cash flow from existing contracts would cover both current and future debt repayments, a financing plan that analysts said was credible. “CoreWeave delivered about the best quarter we could have asked for. Stats were good-to-great, funding concerns were addressed and the strategic moves make sense,” Bernstein analysts led by Madison Rezaei said in a client note. But they warned that CoreWeave “will be among the first and hardest hit” when the crunch in AI computing capacity eases. The risks of mistiming AI investments became evident on Tuesday as SoftBank took a US$3.7 billion writedown on non-refundable payments for equipment to power its U.S. data centres, driving a second-quarter net loss of $7 billion, its first in nearly two years. Nvidia boss Huang’s troubles have left the AI industry reeling too, with the controversy escalating on Tuesday as allegations emerged that his relationship aided multi-billion-dollar Nvidia chip shipments to China. Republican U.S. Senator Kevin Cramer from the Senate Banking Committee called on Huang to step down as CEO. For now, CoreWeave’s results have given investors in AI infrastructure stocks reason to cheer, with Nebius, Iren, Oracle and Applied Digital climbing between six per cent and 14 per cent. All the stocks but Nebius have lost 32 per cent to 48 per cent this year as of Tuesday, while Nebius has surged 60 per cent. Together, the companies, including CoreWeave, were set to gain some $36 billion in market value, while Nvidia alone stood to add nearly $100 billion, if current gains hold. Nebius is due to report results before Thursday’s opening bell. (Reporting by Aditya Soni in Bengaluru; Editing by Devika Syamnath)
